messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj is a 64-year-old warehouse worker who was abducted three years ago while leaving his shift late at night. His captors held him for six hours in a dark, abandoned storage unit, and at one point they threw a burlap sack over his head that he later learned had held snakes—the slithering sensation against his neck was so vivid that even now, the mere mention of a snake in casual conversation makes his stomach drop. The abduction ended when police arrived, but for Raj the night never truly ended.

In the months afterward, Raj began to notice that the same time each evening—around 10:30 PM, when his ordeal began—his body would tense, his heart would race, and he would feel an urgent need to check the locks on every door. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, and he started scanning his surroundings constantly, especially when walking from his truck to the warehouse entrance. At work, he could not stop looking behind him, convinced someone might be following him even though he knew it made no sense. The nighttime itself became a trigger: waking up in the dark, even in his own bedroom, would send a jolt through him, and he would lie still, listening for sounds that weren't there. He started avoiding going to sleep or lying in the dark, staying up until exhaustion forced him into a chair with the television on low. His wife would find him there at dawn, barely asleep.

To cope, Raj began asking his wife repeatedly—sometimes five or six times a night—"Am I okay? Are we safe?" She would reassure him, but it only quieted the fear for a few minutes. He also started checking his own body several times a day: feeling his arms and legs for any sign of injury, pressing on his ribs where he had been kicked, studying his skin in the bathroom mirror at work. That body monitoring kept the memories close, and each time he checked, he thought, *I can't stop bad things from happening to me*—a belief that grew stronger with every reassurance he sought and every sleepless hour he endured. He became certain that if he let himself think about the event in any detail, he would not be able to handle it, so he pushed the thoughts away, but that only made the triggers hit harder. The more he avoided sleep, the more he ended up awake in the dark, reliving the moment the sack was pulled over his head. The more he asked for reassurance, the more he noticed his own vigilance, and the more he checked his body, the more he found signs that something was wrong—a scratch, a bruise, a sore muscle—which sent him back into hypervigilance. A few months ago, Raj started thinking his life was not worth living anymore, though he never told anyone that directly.

Now, Raj is seeking help because his wife told him she can't keep doing the nighttime checks, and his supervisor warned him about distracted behavior on the loading dock. What frightens Raj most is the thought that if he stops checking and scanning, he will be caught off guard again. He hopes that talking to someone might help him sleep through a single night without the dark feeling like a cage.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals cause or increase threat; negative appraisals are shown as consequences of maladaptive strategies and as causes of avoidance, but not as directly influencing threat.
